analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run universal health insurance program covering every American with no copays or deductibles.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 44 cosponsors, was sent to four House committees in March 2003 and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, the children's health program, federal employee coverage, and military family coverage with a single state-administered health program covering every US citizen and lawful resident. It would bar deductibles and copays for most care, stop doctors from billing patients beyond the program's payment, outlaw private insurance that duplicates covered services, and pay for it all with a new payroll tax on employers, a health care income tax, and higher tobacco taxes. It never got past the committee stage.
analysis.who_benefits: Every American who was uninsured or underinsured would gain full coverage with no out-of-pocket costs for doctor visits, hospital care, prescriptions, dental, mental health, and long-term care, and coverage would follow them between jobs and states. Families currently paying premiums would stop; employers would stop paying most of those premiums too.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and everyone with health costs

how_it_helps.text: Every US resident who is a citizen, national, or lawful resident alien would be entitled to benefits under a state-administered program, enrolled automatically at birth or upon gaining lawful status.
The bill prohibits deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments for acute care and preventive benefits, and bars providers from charging patients more than the program pays.

Benefits would be comprehensive, covering hospital care, professional services, prescription drugs, dental care, mental health and substance abuse treatment, preventive services, and long-term care, and would be portable across states.

The program would supersede Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and CHAMPUS, replacing them with a single entitlement funded through an American Health Security Trust Fund.
Financing would come from a payroll tax on employers, a health care income tax, and increased excise taxes on tobacco products.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay a new payroll tax and taxpayers a new health care income tax; smokers would pay higher tobacco taxes. Private health insurers would lose the business of covering basic care, since duplicative insurance would be banned. Hospitals and doctors would face government-set global budgets and fee schedules instead of negotiated insurance rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, taxpayers, insurers, and tobacco companies

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, federal employee health coverage, and CHAMPUS coverage as of the end of 2004, so tens of millions of people would be moved off coverage they know into a new program during a short transition.
The new payroll tax on employers and health care income tax would be a substantial tax increase whose total cost is not specified in the summary.

Long-term care would carry significant cost-sharing: 20 percent coinsurance for home and community-based services and 35 percent for nursing facility services, phased down only for people near the poverty line.
Private health insurance duplicating covered services would be prohibited, so people satisfied with their current coverage could not keep buying it.

Hospitals would be paid from state-approved global budgets and doctors from a prospective fee schedule, which supporters would call cost control and critics would call government rationing of provider payment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For anyone uninsured, underinsured, or facing medical bills, the bill offered near-total elimination of out-of-pocket health costs and universal coverage, paid for by broad new taxes and the end of private basic coverage. The costs are real and large: a major tax shift onto employers and taxpayers, one-time disruption for everyone on Medicare, Medicaid, or employer plans, and significant coinsurance on long-term care. Whether the trade was worth it would depend on whether the government-set budgets paid providers enough to keep care available — a question the bill left to a new standards board.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and then to subcommittees, and no committee ever held a markup or sent it to the floor; the last entry in its record is the sponsor's introductory remarks a year later.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the American Health Security Act of 2003 on March 11, 2003, joined by 17 other members including Reps. Rangel, Stark, Kucinich, Conyers, Waxman, and Sanders.
The House referred the bill to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform, and Armed Services Committees on the day it was introduced.

In late March and April 2003, portions were referred to the Health subcommittee of Energy and Commerce, the Civil Service and Agency Organization subcommittee of Government Reform, and the Health subcommittee of Ways and Means.
The bill attracted 44 cosponsors, 43 Democrats and 1 Independent, all members of the House minority party.
The only subsequent action in the entire Congress was the sponsor's introductory remarks on March 4, 2004; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers kept their existing role and revenue, employers avoided a new payroll tax, and everyone on Medicare, Medicaid, or employer coverage stayed where they were — while the uninsured remained uninsured.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or the House's lone Independent, the bill was introduced by a Democrat, and the Republican-led committees of referral took no action; no vote was ever recorded on it.

industries.note: The bill bans the sale of any private health insurance that duplicates program benefits, effectively ending the industry's core business of covering basic medical care. Insurers' continued revenue depended on the bill dying.

Providers would trade insurance paperwork, unpaid bills, and balance billing for guaranteed payment through global budgets and fee schedules — but those government-set payments would likely be below private rates. Every American would become a guaranteed customer.

Employers would owe a new payroll tax but would shed the far larger cost of providing health benefits, since employer duplicative coverage would be barred. The bill repeals ERISA continuation-coverage rules that currently govern employer plans.

Prescription drugs would be covered for everyone under a Board-set payment schedule, expanding the customer base while eliminating private-negotiated prices. The bill preserves antitrust exemptions for independent pharmacy reimbursement discussions.
The bill raises excise taxes on tobacco products to help fund coverage, adding cost at the point of sale for smokers and manufacturers.
